claims.text: WAL's throughput advantage over rollback journal does not collapse from write concurrency itself—both modes serialize writes through a single-writer lock. WAL's advantage comes from decoupling readers from writers. The throughput advantage collapses when sustained writes combine with concurrent long-running read transactions: the long readers prevent checkpoints, the WAL file grows unbounded, and all readers slow proportionally as they search the growing WAL for pages. Checkpoint starvation is the most common production failure of the whole WAL subsystem, and recognizing it allows targeted fixes like enforcing reader timeouts instead of changing database architecture.

claims.text: Both WAL and rollback journal serialize writes through a single-writer lock, so neither mode provides concurrent write throughput over the other. Rollback journal fails immediately under concurrent read-write workloads with SQLITE_BUSY errors because readers block writers. WAL achieves higher read throughput but fails at checkpoint starvation caused by long-running readers, leading to unbounded WAL file growth. The mode choice depends on your reader concurrency pattern, not write volume: use WAL if you have many concurrent short readers; avoid WAL if you have few but long-running queries.

claims.text: Production WAL deployments should monitor WAL file size growth and checkpoint frequency as forward-looking signals of checkpoint starvation. Rising WAL file size indicates long-running readers are blocking checkpoints; early detection allows operators to enforce query timeouts, tune wal_autocheckpoint to trigger checkpoints more frequently, or schedule checkpoints during reader gaps—interventions that prevent unbounded WAL growth and the read performance degradation that follows. Without this monitoring, operators discover the problem only after SQLITE_BUSY or SQLITE_FULL errors surface, at which point performance has already collapsed.

claims.text: PostgreSQL generates approximately 3.5 times more WAL when indexes exist during bulk insert operations compared to creating the same indexes after data insertion. This occurs because the database must log every individual index modification as rows arrive, whereas post-insertion indexing writes larger sequential blocks to WAL.

claims.text: PostgreSQL operators should retain 3 to 5 days of WAL; unused replication slots or slow subscribers cause WAL segments to accumulate without limit since old segments cannot be recycled until all active replication slots have consumed them. The restart_lsn metric in pg_replication_slots directly indicates how far back each slot requires WAL to extend.
